question: What is the primary characteristic of inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: Gradual deterioration of tissues driven by genetic mutations
options.B: Sudden onset of symptoms triggered by viral pathogens
options.C: Temporary functional loss caused by nutritional deficiencies
options.D: Reversible tissue damage resulting from acute trauma

explanation: These conditions involve permanent genetic alterations that cause progressive functional decline in organs or tissues over time. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h1)

question: Why is early recognition of hereditary disorders challenging in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Genetic mutations automatically reverse themselves spontaneously
options.B: Patients completely lack any physical or psychological symptoms
options.C: Symptoms often mimic common non-genetic illnesses initially
options.D: Hereditary conditions only affect individuals over the age of ninety

explanation: Early clinical presentations are frequently vague, leading to potential misattribution before specialized diagnostic workups are performed. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h1)

question: How many generations are typically included in a standard clinical pedigree chart?
explanation: A standard medical pedigree maps out at least three generations to clearly establish patterns of inherited traits within a family line. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h2)

question: A nurse constructing a family history chart notices a pattern of a condition appearing exclusively through maternal lines. What does this suggest?

options.A: An X-linked or mitochondrial mode of inheritance
options.B: An acquired infectious disease spread through casual contact
options.C: A completely random genetic mutation with no family link
options.D: An environmental toxin exposure limited to workplaces

explanation: Specific transmission paths across generations provide strong clues regarding how a mutant gene is passed down. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of primary prevention strategies in genetics?

options.A: Preventing the initial occurrence of disease manifestations
options.C: Managing chronic pain in hospitalized patients

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping a health condition from developing before any pathological changes begin. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h3)

question: Which nursing intervention represents a primary prevention activity for inherited disorders?

options.A: Administering physical therapy for muscle wasting
options.B: Providing premarital education on genetic compatibility
options.C: Performing diagnostic biopsies on symptomatic patients
options.D: Prescribing palliative medications for end-stage failure

explanation: Educating couples before marriage or conception allows them to assess hereditary risks and make choices that avoid passing severe disorders to offspring. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h3)

question: What defines an individual who is a carrier for an autosomal recessive disorder?

options.A: They are completely immune to all forms of genetic mutations
options.B: They exhibit severe clinical symptoms of the active disease
options.C: They carry two copies of the mutated gene on their sex chromosomes
options.D: They possess one copy of the mutated gene and are usually healthy

explanation: Carriers have a single altered gene paired with a normal gene, which typically protects them from the disease while leaving them able to transmit the trait. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h4)

question: A couple discovers through screening that both are carriers for an autosomal recessive condition. What is the statistical chance per pregnancy that their child will inherit two copies of the mutated gene?
explanation: When two carriers conceive, standard Mendelian inheritance dictates a one-in-four or 25 percent probability that the child inherits both recessive alleles. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h4)

question: What is the main objective of secondary prevention in inherited disorders?

options.A: Preventing parents from ever conceiving children
options.B: Providing terminal comfort care in hospital settings
options.C: Early detection and prompt intervention to limit disease progression
options.D: Eliminating the mutated gene entirely from the human population

explanation: Secondary prevention catches conditions early through screening so treatments can be initiated before severe, permanent harm occurs. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h5)

question: Which factor represents the greatest risk to the success of newborn screening programs?

options.A: Breakdowns in follow-up systems to connect positive results with care
options.B: Excessive availability of advanced genetic therapy clinics
options.C: Immediate reporting of test results to attending physicians
options.D: High public compliance with routine immunization schedules

explanation: A positive screening test is useless if the healthcare system fails to track down the family and initiate treatment promptly. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h5)

question: What is a common psychological response experienced by families receiving a diagnosis of an inherited degenerative disorder?

options.A: Immediate relief and total indifference to long-term health
options.B: Complete physical immunity to secondary infections
options.C: Euphoria over discovering unique family traits
options.D: Guilt and anxiety regarding passing the condition to offspring

explanation: Discovering a hereditary condition often triggers complex emotional reactions, including self-blame and worry for children. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a core ethical responsibility of the nurse in genetic care?

options.A: Advocating for the patient's right to make autonomous choices
options.B: Protecting the privacy and confidentiality of genetic test results
options.C: Providing unbiased information regarding reproductive options
options.D: Forcing mandatory genetic testing on reluctant family members

explanation: Coercion violates patient autonomy; nursing practice strictly upholds voluntary participation and informed consent in genetic testing. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h6)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team essential for managing inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: Patients with genetic disorders require permanent hospitalization
options.B: Single practitioners possess absolute cures for genetic mutations
options.C: These complex conditions affect multiple body systems over a long period
options.D: Specialized teams eliminate the need for any nursing involvement

explanation: Because degeneration touches physical, nutritional, and emotional domains, diverse specialists must collaborate to provide comprehensive care. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h7)

question: What is a primary responsibility of the nurse within a multidisciplinary genetic care team?

options.A: Independently prescribing all specialized pharmaceutical therapies
options.B: Performing surgical interventions for advanced tissue degeneration
options.C: Coordinating communication and care activities among various specialists
options.D: Replacing the geneticist in formulating final chromosomal diagnoses

explanation: Nurses frequently serve as the central hub connecting different disciplines, ensuring that the patient's holistic care plan is seamlessly executed. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h7)
